rv.q: This revival, by director and choreographer Camille A. Brown, is the most essential production of Shange’s masterwork to date.
It pulses and pulses with life, singing a Black girl’s song.
Each cast member is as compelling as the next, some of their segments more impressionistic than narrative.
The production, which opens April 20, takes the task of revival seriously — it's a joy to witness.
This production doesn't just honor Shange's work; it amplifies it, finding new frequencies in familiar words.

"This version of 'for colored girls' truly does feel like a choreopoem, Shange’s term for her amalgamation of words, motion and music. (The percussive original score is by Martha Redbone and Aaron Whitby).
This revival feels both timeless and urgently contemporary, with a cast that brings fresh fire to familiar wounds.

The vibrant new revival, directed and choreographed by Camille A. Brown, recaptures the show’s pioneering, even radical spirit; it remains a show that stands apart, even as explorations of black experience have proliferated in the theater in the years since.
Her words have become more than the unspoken and unrealized accounts of Black women's pain and promise; they have evolved into the gift of permission to heal and the agency to be seen and understood.

The best moments in this production, which features the performers Amara Granderson, Tendayi Kuumba, Kenita R. Miller, Okwui Okpokwasili, Stacey Sargeant, Alexandria Wailes and D Woods, are those when the words face forward, the speaker tells truths, and the lyrical beauty of the piece is allowed to...
The play comes across, unfortunately, as an antiquated time machine that’s at odds with the current conversation.
The revival of Ntozake Shange’s 1976 for colored girls who have considered suicide/when the rainbow is enuf is stunning in every aspect.
If there is any theatre justice, it will remain there for a very long time.
The women’s exuberance, their togetherness, their loyalty to each other, their love for each other, is sustaining for them and a bracing, life-imparting thing to watch for us.
I wholeheartedly welcome this superb, long-overdue revival of Shange's singular 'choreopoem'
The sounds of humanity are what pierce through.
Shange’s cycle of poetic monologues finds a way to put a rainbow of vibrant color back in what can often be a very bleak world.
If the poetic language may sometimes be too dense and quick for full comprehension, the rhythm always gets you through.

Brown, who has become the first Black woman to serve as a director-choreographer on Broadway in 65 years, was an ideal choice for helming the revival, infusing it with modern dance and coordinating its visual and lyrical elements into a striking pattern.
Somehow Brown has found a way to keep Shange’s work both mysterious and accessible—quite an accomplishment.
No one asks, Are you okay? because these women are beyond platitudes.
That is the tragedy of this production: Brown has arranged many glorious moments, but their potential remains unfulfilled.
It’s not an ideal production, but if you can focus on the words themselves rather than the other stimuli thrown your way, it remains essential, vivid, and affirming.
This new vibrant, energetic production from director-choreographer Camille A. Brown celebrates the play's spirit of sisterhood with joyous movement and magnificent acting.
The generosity with which the play shares its worlds with the women watching it is its greatest strength.

cn.t: Critics hail Camille A. Brown's vibrant revival of Shange's groundbreaking choreopoem as triumphant and urgent, praising strong performances and dynamic choreography, though a few find it uneven or question its contemporary relevance.

sg.ra: The Booth is one of Broadway's smallest houses at 766 seats, so center orchestra rows C-H give close-up detail of plays and intimate dramas without paying the very-front premium. Row AA front offers max legroom (Headout) but stage is high; step back a few rows for better sightline onto the stage floor.

sg.vl: Workable angle, not the sweet spot
sg.ra: Booth is narrow so side orchestra remains viable, but a 2018 BWW forum post specifically flagged 'angle from the front side seats' as a concern. Closer rows (BB, A) on the side get awkward angles onto the high stage. Mid-house aisle seats recover the view while adding legroom.
sg.rr: A-P (17 rows, odd 1-15 left, even 2-16 right)

sg.ra: In a 252-seat mezzanine with only 8 rows, even the back row is close. SeatPlan and Headout both call Center Mezz A-B some of the best seats in the house, and G-H are cited as strong value. With the Booth's intimate scale, the mezzanine never feels distant — this is the value pick.

sg.vl: Small house saves the side angle
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly notes side-mezz views are 'slightly more angled but still viable' because the Booth is narrow. Decent budget alternative, but the center mezz is a better value at similar price tier so this is solid-not-sweet.
